Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self Assessment.

images.text:
I have been told a Chinese folk tale about a farmer and a horse. It is being passed on a lot these days here in China. It has been recounted by a teacher I work with. It has even been talked about while I was taking a yoga class! It isn't being called a myth, even though it's 2000 years old.

It isn't being spoken of as a legend, either. Obviously it has been around for ages! Let me unlock the mystery and begin! I have been asked to write it here, so I got one of my students to tell the story again ...

My student told me that a farmer had received a horse. He asked me if I thought this was good news, and I agreed it might be.

Then he told me that the horse went away and brought another one back with him to their abode. He said that the farmer humbly thanked the horse, bowing deeply. He asked me if I thought this was good news, and again I agreed it might be.

It seems the farmer gave the second horse to his son, who rode it, was thrown off, and broke his leg. A concerned neighbor conveys that he is sorry to hear this. Whether it's good news, or bad news, the farmer cannot say.

A week or later, the emperor's launches a war. All able-bodied young men are taken away to fight. The farmer's son cannot. This is good news, of course!

You use reported speech (indirect speech) when you are saying (reporting) what other people said.
This style of writing is common in storytelling. It allows the writer to share dialogue with the reader without always using quotation marks.

When you tell people what someone has said you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past' since we are reporting the information at a later time. You need to change the verb to the next past form.

You have to change the pronoun if you are reporting what someone else said. Compare these two sentences. In each case the person actually said "I don't want to go."

• I said, “I don't want to go.” > I said (that) I didn't want to go.
  • Bill said, “I don't want to go.” > Bill said (that) he didn't want to go.
When you want to report questions asked, the subject normally comes before the verb.

Direct: Where is the sun?
Indirect: The wind asked where the sun was.
When the question is a yes/no questions, you use if or whether to report it.
He asked me if/whether I thought this was good news, and again I agreed it might be.

The Passive: The Present Continuous and Present Perfect Tenses

You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
People are not speaking of it as a legend.

You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.
Someone has told me about a Chinese folktale about a farmer and a horse.
You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in storytelling.
Look at the chart below for the structure of the passive voice.
